title: The world is urbanizing fast — the window to get it right is narrowing
gist: World Bank urban leads argue the decisive urbanization decisions of this century are being made now in small, fiscally weak cities in Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia, not megacities: 4.7bn people (58%) are urban today and 70%+ by 2050, built-up area grows 50%+ in 25 years, and slum dwellers rose from ~840m in 2018 to over 1bn by 2022. Their core claim is that the urban wage premium is largely absorbed by rents, so the welfare case for cities depends entirely on planning housing and transport ahead of growth.

insights.claim: 4.7 billion people, about 58 percent of the world's population, live in urban areas today, and that share crosses 70 percent by 2050.
insights.so_what: The baseline for any long-horizon infrastructure, cement, power and housing demand model — the marginal urban resident for the next 25 years is the demand story.
insights.quote: Today, 4.7 billion people, about 58 percent of the world's population, live in urban areas. By 2050, that share will cross 70 percent.
insights.speaker: @worldbank

insights.claim: The bulk of coming urban growth will occur not in megacities but in rapidly spreading smaller cities, concentrated in Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia where planning capacity is weakest and fiscal resources thinnest.
insights.so_what: Capital and infrastructure exposure should tilt toward secondary-city delivery models rather than megacity marquee projects; the addressable market is fragmented and low-capacity.
insights.quote: The next chapter of urbanization will be defined by the rapid spread of smaller cities across the globe, many of them in Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia, where planning capacity is weakest and fiscal resources are thinnest.
insights.locator: The bulk of that growth won't happen in megacities
insights.speaker: @worldbank

insights.claim: The most consequential urban decisions of the century are being taken right now in cities that are not household names, implying that policy attention aimed at famous megacities is misallocated.
insights.so_what: Signals a coming reallocation of development finance and donor attention toward small-city planning mandates.
insights.quote: The most important urban decisions of this century are being made right now, mostly in cities you've never heard of.
insights.speaker: @worldbank

themes.theme: Thick labor markets as the real jobs case

insights.claim: The jobs case for cities rests on labor-market thickness — more firms competing for workers and more occupations — which gives workers sector-switching optionality that functions as job security without formal contracts.
insights.so_what: A reusable lens for judging which cities absorb shocks: density of employer competition, not formal-contract coverage, predicts local labor resilience.
insights.quote: That is job security of a particular kind, one that has nothing to do with formal contracts and everything to do with density.
insights.locator: Cities offer workers something rural areas
insights.speaker: @worldbank

insights.claim: The standard urban productivity argument focuses on firms — agglomeration, knowledge spillovers, lower trade costs — but the authors deliberately start the case from workers instead.
insights.so_what: Reframes urban investment appraisal around household welfare and labor optionality rather than firm-level productivity, changing which projects clear the bar.
insights.quote: The standard argument for urban productivity focuses on firms: agglomeration, knowledge spillovers, lower trade costs. All true. But the jobs argument starts somewhere else.
insights.locator: Why the jobs case for cities is stronger than it looks
insights.speaker: @worldbank

insights.claim: Skilled workers learn faster when surrounded by peers with similar or complementary skills, which raises urban productivity and reinforces cities as engines of economic growth.
insights.so_what: Supports the durability of urban wage premia in skill-dense clusters even as low-skill urban gains get eroded by living costs.
insights.speaker: @worldbank

insights.claim: In low- and middle-income economies, low-wage informal urban jobs function as a skills ladder, but the ladder only works if the city supplies housing, transport and services that make the next rung reachable.
insights.so_what: Identifies the precise failure mode — missing urban services — that converts informal work from mobility into a poverty trap; a screen for which cities generate a consuming middle class.
insights.quote: when the city lacks the housing, transport, and services that make the next rung accessible, the steppingstone becomes a landing.
insights.locator: The informal economy in an African or South Asian city
insights.speaker: @worldbank

themes.theme: Rents eat the urban wage premium

insights.claim: Higher urban wages often do little more than offset the added expense of city living, with rents absorbing the premium, so the measured wage gap overstates the real welfare gain from urbanization.
insights.so_what: Urbanization rates alone are a poor proxy for rising real consumer purchasing power in frontier markets; housing supply elasticity is the variable to track.
insights.quote: The complication: higher urban wages often do little more than offset the added expenses of city living. Rents absorb the premium.
insights.speaker: @worldbank

insights.claim: Whether cities improve welfare is conditional on planning quality keeping housing and commute costs from consuming the earnings gain, making planning — not density itself — the binding variable.
insights.so_what: Gives a testable screen for city-level investment: track housing and transport cost trajectories, not headline wage or GDP growth.
insights.quote: The jobs case for cities, on welfare grounds, ultimately depends on whether the city is planned well enough to keep housing and commute costs from eating the earnings gain.
insights.speaker: @worldbank

insights.claim: Nearly one in four urban residents worldwide live in slum conditions, with the heaviest concentration in low-income countries.
insights.so_what: Sets the scale of the unserved urban services market — sanitation, tenure, drainage — that development finance will target.
insights.quote: Nearly one in four urban residents around the world live in slum conditions, many of them in low-income countries.
insights.speaker: @worldbank

insights.claim: The global number of slum dwellers rose from approximately 840 million in 2018 to over one billion by 2022, an increase of more than 160 million people in four years.
insights.so_what: Absolute deterioration despite falling shares — the direction of travel argues for larger, faster urban upgrading budgets than headline ratios suggest.
insights.quote: globally, the number of slum dwellers grew from approximately 840 million in 2018 to over one billion by 2022, an increase of more than 160 million people in just four years.
insights.locator: The aggregate number is what should alarm planners
insights.speaker: @worldbank

insights.claim: In Sub-Saharan Africa the slum population share fell from more than 60 percent to just over 50 percent over twenty years but has been rising again since 2020, reversing two decades of progress.
insights.so_what: A post-2020 inflection worth watching — it implies urban service delivery lost ground through the pandemic and inflation period.
insights.quote: In Sub-Saharan Africa, the slum population fell from more than 60 percent to just over 50 percent over twenty years. The share has been rising again since 2020.
insights.locator: That fraction sounds like it should be falling
insights.speaker: @worldbank

insights.claim: A falling slum share inside a rapidly growing city still increases the absolute number of people in inadequate conditions — the distributional trick that aggregate urbanization statistics routinely conceal.
insights.so_what: A general warning against ratio-based development metrics; size the market off absolute headcounts, not percentages.
insights.quote: This is the distributional trick that aggregate urbanization statistics routinely conceal.
insights.locator: A falling slum share in a rapidly growing city
insights.speaker: @worldbank

themes.theme: Path dependence: build now or pay for fifty years

insights.claim: Urban built-up area — buildings, roads and paved land — is projected to grow by more than 50 percent over the next 25 years, largely in lower-middle and upper-middle income countries.
insights.so_what: A structural, multi-decade demand signal for cement, steel, aggregates, paving and drainage, concentrated in middle-income markets rather than the poorest or richest.
insights.quote: Urban built-up areas, the land surface covered by human-made structures and surfaces, including buildings, roads, and paved land, are projected to grow by more than 50 percent over the next 25 years
insights.speaker: @worldbank

insights.claim: Addis Ababa grew from fewer than one million residents in 1975 to over 6.7 million by 2025, with planned and unplanned zones distinguishable today by road connectivity, drainage quality and formal tenure.
insights.so_what: A concrete, observable diagnostic — connectivity, drainage, tenure — for grading any fast-growing city's future service costs.
insights.quote: In 1975, fewer than one million people lived there. By 2025, its population exceeded 6.7 million.
insights.locator: Addis Ababa shows what happens both ways
insights.speaker: @worldbank

insights.claim: Productive and dysfunctional cities are not different types of city but the same city governed differently, meaning governance quality — not geography or income level — determines whether agglomeration benefits materialize.
insights.so_what: Argues city-level governance is the primary risk factor to underwrite in municipal or urban infrastructure exposure.
insights.quote: The productive city and the dysfunctional city are not different types. They are the same city, governed differently, across the same decades.
insights.locator: A fragmented city, where housing, jobs, and services are disconnected
insights.speaker: @worldbank

insights.claim: Road layouts, land tenure systems and drainage standards being installed in African cities right now will determine municipal fiscal capacity and service quality for the next fifty years.
insights.so_what: Long-duration lock-in: today's cheap shortcuts become tomorrow's permanent municipal liabilities, a credit consideration for sub-sovereign debt.
insights.quote: the physical infrastructure going into African cities right now, the road layouts, the land tenure systems, the drainage standards, will determine fiscal capacity and service quality for the next fifty years.
insights.locator: This is the argument for urgency
insights.speaker: @worldbank

insights.claim: Retrofitting urban form becomes exponentially harder once informal settlements consolidate and the political economy of land calcifies around incumbent occupants, so the reform window closes on its own.
insights.so_what: Time-decay on policy optionality: interventions priced today are far cheaper than the same fix later, favoring front-loaded urban capex.
insights.quote: Getting the block size wrong in Kampala in 2026 means paying for it in 2076.
insights.locator: Reforming it will be exponentially harder
insights.speaker: @worldbank

insights.claim: Because large parts of Sub-Saharan Africa's urban environment have yet to be built, today's planning and investment decisions carry unusually durable influence over future productivity and opportunity.
insights.so_what: Frames the region as the highest-leverage, highest-optionality urban market globally — and the one where policy failure compounds longest.
insights.quote: The choices available today won't be available tomorrow.
insights.speaker: @worldbank
